title: fix: fix middleware request routing
description:
Fix #51. Since Connect [2024.11.0](https://docs.posit.co/connect/news/#posit-connect-2024.11.0-fixed), FastAPI applications receive `scope["path"]` as the full content URL (e.g. `/content/<guid>/evaluate`) rather than the path relative to the content mount point (e.g. `/evaluate`). The Tableau middleware was doing a naive `scope["path"] == "/evaluate"` check, so it never matched and requests to `/evaluate` 404'd.

I had to also make some other updates to places where the codebase relied on deprecated or internal APIs that broke with recent versions of python, fastapi, and starlette. I've updated our CI matrix as well.

description:

Some Connect `rsconnect-python` deployment tests failed for `fastapitableau` which lead me here to try to find a fix.

Addresses #48

The latest `fastapi` has an incompatability with `fastapitableau`

### Solution

- Pin to the last know compatible version of `fastapi`
- Also pin to a known compatibile version of `httpx` which appears to be used in testing only

Otherwise `fastapitableau` will need code changes to work with the very latest versions of these dependencies.

## Testing Notes / Validation Steps

All tests should pass

```

pipenv install --dev
just test
```

title: Test against latest FastAPI
description:
## Description

CI adjustments.

- Added Python 3.12 to all workflows.
- Added a new workflow, "Test Latest FastAPI", which sets up a dev environment and runs tests. It is similar to the CI workflow, with a few differences:
  - Skips linting.
  - Before running the tests, it runs `pip install --upgrade fastapi`, which installs the latest FastAPI, despite it being pinned by FastAPI-Tableau to an earlier version.
  - Scheduled to run every Monday at 1:00 PM UTC (9 AM EDT).

Ideally, this workflow will fail when we break on the latest FastAPI, giving us a heads-up that updating to the latest FastAPI will require changes.

Right now, Pip prints a message about the dependency conflict but does not prevent the upgrade. It is possible that future versions of Pip will prevent this "breaking" upgrade. If that happens, we might need to use a tool like [tox](https://tox.wiki/en/latest/).

## Testing Notes / Validation Steps

N/A; CI change only.

title: Support latest FastAPI and Pydantic 2.0
description:
## Description

Updates FastAPI-Tableau to support the latest (at time of writing) version of FastAPI and Pydantic 2.0.

Here are a summary of changes:

- In `routing.py`, updated `TableauRoute`'s code that gets its own schema.
  - We use the schema to validate requests against the schema and rewrite Tableau-style requests to match what FastAPI expects.
  - Pydantic 2.0 changed or removed some of the capabilities FastAPI used to get this information. We mirrored FastAPI's use of those functions. FastAPI now uses functions from an internal module named `_compat`. We import functions from that internal module.
- Update `user_guide.py` to correctly populate parameters from endpoints.
  - When constructing our user guide, we used to use an internal method of endpoint parameters called `_type_display()`. This has moved to `pydantic._internal._repr` as `display_as_type()`.
  - Added tests to ensure that parameters are properly populated.
- Some other small modifications to account for upstream changes, add type annotations, etc.
- Re-vendor and modify OpenAPI function from FastAPI (now OpenAPI v5 rather than v3 I think).
- Modify docs URLs that have changed.

Originally, I wanted to vendor some of the internal functions we call, after discussing with @mmarchetti. When I investigated more closely, the amount of code I'd have to vendor was significantly higher than we first thought. Instead, I'm going to pin to the current FastAPI version. I think this is a legitimate approach, as this is designed to be a replacement, rather than a supplement, to FastAPI.

Following on from this PR, I'll try to set a GitHub Action that tests against newer-than-pinned versions of FastAPI and Pydantic so we can monitor for breakages.

Addresses #37 

## Testing Notes / Validation Steps

We should ensure that all our demo content can be published to Connect and works with Tableau as expected. More detailed testing notes to come.

title: Add debug logging capabilities
description: ## Description Addresses #24 ### Problem FastAPI Tableau does not have the debug logging capabilities that plumbertableau has. We want a user to be able to enable more verbose logging in the app's log panel (or to their local console) with the presence of a specific environment variable. ### Solution If a user sets the environment variable `FASTAPITABLEAU_LOG_LEVEL` to `DEBUG` (case-insensitive), FastAPI Tableau will emit log messages for certain events. These include: - Generating OpenAPI schemas (Tableau and regular-style) - Generating Tableau setup and usage instructions - Responding to an `/info` request - Receiving any request scope in `TableauExtensionMiddleware` - Receiving the body for a request in `TableauExtensionMiddleware` - Rewriting the path of a scope in `TableauExtensionMiddleware` - Not rewriting the body of a request to a `TableauRoute` - Rewriting the body of a request to a `TableauRoute` - The extension checks to see whether it's running on Connect - Any warning message is added to the list of warning messages If the logger is passed a scope as `extra` information, it will check to see if that scope contains a correlation ID in its headers (looking for the keys `x-rs-correlation-id` and `x-correlation-id`). If that header exists, it'll prepend it to that log message. I added tests to ensure that logs print and include a correlation ID, and also that they don't print when the log level is set to its default (`WARNING`). I didn't test every single log message's text. ### Other changes - Got optional HTTP support for warning messages working, also keyed off an environment variable. - Replaced relative imports with absolute imports. - The license was incorrectly listed as "Proprietary" in the package's metadata, even though the license file was always MIT. - The routing tests weren't actually running because you need a special package, like `pytest-asyncio`. Got them working. - We were cross-linking between Tableau and regular-style OpenAPI docs, but that doesn't work on Connect, so I removed it. ## Testing Notes / Validation Steps I validated that log messages were correctly printing when I ran the package locally during development. I also published content to a YETI server with a late commit from this branch and verified that debug messages were printing correctly to the logs panel (and included correlation IDs).

title: Support defining endpoints with Pydantic schemas
description:
## Description

This pull request adds support for defining schemas with Pydantic models. It addresses #22.

### Problem

Previously, you could not define endpoints using Pydantic models. This was a problem in particular because FastAPI's documentation *leads* with Pydantic models.

This was because of the way we handled Tableau requests.

When we get a request from Tableau, we know the endpoint it is sent to, but not what arguments the items in its body are supposed to be assigned to. We want to essentially pass them to the Python function's arguments in order, rather than by keyword, by renaming `_arg1`, `_arg2`, … , `argn` with the names that the Python function expects.

We used to do this by examining the list of body parameters in `route.dependant.body_params`, which, if they have been defined as normal function arguments, have a `name` property we can use. However, if a Pydantic model has been used, we just see the name of the model's class, which isn't helpful.

### Solution

This update changes the way that body parameter names are looked up to one that uses FastAPI and Pydantic functions to create a schema for a TableauRoute that contains the information we need.

This schema dict is generated by two functions. The first, `TableauRoute.get_body_field_schema()`, follows a pattern established by Pydantic and FastAPI (which I won't go into here) to get data about the endpoint's body field. It returns a tuple of a schema, the any definitions therein, and nested models. We don't call this directly right now — we access it via the property `TableauRoute.body_schema`, which is actually a function that either generates and stores the body schema using the above function, or retrieves the stored body schema. 

This allows us to change our `TableauRoute.custom_route_handler()` and its auxiliary `TableauRoute.rewrite_request_body()` methods. The latter has been renamed to `TableauRoute.ensure_request_body()` because it doesn't rewrite every request body, only ones that look like they came from Tableau.

`TableauRoute.ensure_request_body()` now first tries to call FastAPI's function to unpack the body arguments. If that succeeds, it does not do anything to the request body. Otherwise, it operates on request bodies that are dicts with keys named `script` and `data`. It checks the `body_schema` property to see what the endpoint expects, and tries to modify the data accordingly. (It's easier to read the function than my written description of it).

### Other Changes

- Factored out the code that consumes an entire event from `receive()`, since we use it in multiple places. It's now in `utils.py`.
- Modified the justfile's `serve` recipe to look by default in an external directory that the user can specify. This is because we don't keep scratch files in the repo any more.
- Wrote new tests for the above code. We check that Pydantic and argument-defined endpoints correctly rewrite Tableau requests and leave regular ones alone.

## Testing Notes / Validation Steps

This app contains four endpoints, with single- and multiple-parameter versions, defined using arguments and with a Pydantic schema respectively. You should be able to view the OpenAPI (Tableau) documentation and successfully submit Tableau-style requests from there.

```python
from typing import List
from pydantic import BaseModel

from fastapitableau import FastAPITableau

app = FastAPITableau(
    title="Simple Example",
    description="A *simple* example FastAPITableau app.",
    version="0.1.0",
)

class SingleArg(BaseModel):
    text: List[str]

@app.post("/capitalize_pyd")
def capitalize_pyd(item: SingleArg) -> List[str]:
    capitalized = [t.upper() for t in item.text]
    return capitalized


class TwoArgs(BaseModel):
    first: List[str]
    second: List[str]

@app.post("/paste_pyd")
def paste_pyd(item: TwoArgs) -> List[str]:
    result = [a + " " + b for a, b in zip(item.first, item.second)]
    return result


@app.post("/capitalize_arg")
def capitalize_arg(text: List[str]) -> List[str]:
    capitalized = [t.upper() for t in text]
    return capitalized


@app.post("/paste_arg")
def paste_arg(first: List[str], second: List[str]) -> List[str]:
    result = [a + " " + b for a, b in zip(first, second)]
    return result
```

title: Fix handling of large JSON bodies
description:
Addresses https://github.com/rstudio/connect/issues/19982

### Problem

FastAPI Tableau would fail on large JSON bodies.

### Solution

Added proper functionality to handle long async requests. The Middleware now consumes the entire request event properly.

### Other Changes

This PR contains other changes:

- `replace_dict_keys()` used to take a simple list of new keys. This could cause problems — if any old keys were the same as new keys, it could lead to deletion or unintended re-ordering. Now it requires a dict explicitly mapping old keys to new keys, as in `{"old_key": "new_key"}`. I rewrote the places where it's called to generate the key map.
- The user guide used to fail to render if a function didn't have a defined return type. Now it displays a warning message instead of the Tableau copy-and-paste function.
- The Tableau OpenAPI docs used to fail to build if a function took the entire Request as its input. Now it is just not rewritten.

title: Initial implementation of Tableau-friendly exception handlers
description:
This PR adds exception handlers that format all returned exceptions in a Tableau-friendly manner. It also includes a few other misc changes.

### Exception handling

There are two special case exception handlers for `HTTPException` and `RequestValidationError`, and a general fallback for all other `Exception`s.

All exceptions are returned as JSON objects, with a `message` property containing `Server Error: [Python Exception subclass name]` and more detail in an `info` property. For example:

```bash
❯ curl -X 'POST' \
      'http://127.0.0.1:8000/evaluate' \
      -H 'accept: application/json' \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d '{
          "script": "/fail",
          "data": {
                  "arg1_": ["rabbit"]
          }
  }' -i
HTTP/1.1 420
date: Thu, 23 Sep 2021 15:37:41 GMT
server: uvicorn
content-length: 52
content-type: application/json

{"message":"Server Error","info":"This didn't work"}


❯ curl -X 'POST' \
      'http://127.0.0.1:8000/fail' \
      -H 'accept: application/json' \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d '{
          "first": ["Toph", "Bill", "James"]
  }'
{"message":"Server Error: RequestValidationError","info":"1 validation error for Request\nbody\n  value is not a valid list (type=type_error.list)"}
```

The special cases for RequestValidationError and HTTPException work around the fact that they contain `.detail` properties that aren't included when you run `str(exception)`, and that they imply specific error codes.

The fallback, registered for all `Exception`s, means that any error occurring in the server _should_ be sent back in a Tableau-friendly manner.

### Other changes

- Moved `get_swagger_ui_html()` to `openapi.py`.

title: Rewrite OpenAPI schema to contain Tableau-style example requests
description:
### Problem

Generated OpenAPI schema does not contain Tableau-style example requests.

### Solution

This PR contains a few extra things generated as I was working on this, including some scratch files and an example or two. The important things are under the `fastapitableau` directory.

#### `fastapitableau/applications.py`

The `FastAPITableau` class now has its own `openapi()`  method. This method calls the original function, then calls the imported `rewrite_tableau_openapi()` function on it, imported from `openapi.py`. It saves this modified object to the default `self.openapi_schema` property.

#### `fastapitableau/openapi.py`

Contains the function that does the rewriting.

This function is a little long, because FastAPI treats single property and multi-property bodies differently. Multi-property bodies (like our example's `/paste` endpoint) are embedded in an object, with argument names from their underlying function as keys. But single-property bodies (like our example's `/capitalize` endpoint) just expect a single object (e.g. a list of strings) in the JSON request body. But when Tableau sends requests, both of these types of objects will be presented in the same way.

The function iterates over the keys in the schema's `paths` dictionary. (TODO: Only operate on TableauRoute paths). On line 16 of this file, there's a conditional block that detects non-embedded single-property bodies, and replicates the type of embedded schema we get with paths that expect multi-property request bodies. Once this block completes, on line 45, both types of request bodies are treated the same.

For each path:

- It renames the keys in the original request body schema to Tableau's argument names.
- It creates a new schema for that path, appending the `_tableau` suffix to its name. This represents the top level of the Tableau request. This schema's `data` property contains a `$ref` to the original schema with the renamed keys.
- It rewrites the `path` entry's `$ref` to point to the new Tableau request schema.

By default, the function will rewrite every path in an OpenAPI schema. However, it accepts an optional argument `rewrite_paths`, a list of strings. If this is present, it will only rewrite those paths. When a `TableauFastAPI instance` calls this function, it passes in a list of its paths which are instances of `TableauRoute`, so any non-Tableau compatible routes will be left intact.

The function uses `copy.deepcopy()` on the dictionary it receives. This means that if we decide to offer both versions of the schema in the future, we will be able to. Before I added this, it would return a dict object, but that was just a reference to the same object that was passed in, which was modified. Now it returns a new dict.

### Testing Notes / Validation Steps

I have tested serving our `simple.py` example. With these changes, it shows Tableau-style request bodies in the OpenAPI docs. This exercises both the forms of schema I aimed to support.
